divisions.question: Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill (No. 1) 2014 - in Committee - Control orders only if support/facilitation already provided

The majority disagreed that a [definition](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2014-11-26.24.1) of the '[Convention Against Torture](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_Against_Torture)' should be inserted into the [Intelligence Services Act 2001](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence_Services_Act_2001), which was proposed by Greens Senator [Penny Wright](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/sa/penny_wright). Attorney General [George Brandis](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/queensland/george_brandis) [said](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2014-11-26.26.1) that it was an unnecessary amendment. ### Background to the bill This [bill](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/s982) is the third that has been introduced since mid-2014. A number of incidents have happened before and during the course of the introduction of these bills. There was [one of the biggest counter-terrorism operations](http://www.abc.net.au/news/2014-09-18/authorities-thwart-beheading-plot-in-australias-biggest-raid/5754276) in Australian history. The Prime Minister [Tony Abbott](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/warringah/tony_abbott) also confirmed that Australia would be [sending the military to Iraq](http://www.abc.net.au/news/2014-10-15/special-forces-could-move-into-iraq-within-days-abbott/5815534) to fight the [Islamic State](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_State_of_Iraq_and_the_Levant) (IS) (also known as the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) or the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL)). The scope of this bill is narrower than the earlier two but some of its measures are "significant and warrant close scrutiny" (see [bills digest](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1415a/15bd050)). In particular, the proposed expansion of the [control order](http://www.ag.gov.au/NationalSecurity/Counterterrorismlaw/Pages/Controlorders.aspx)

The majority disagreed that a [new section](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2014-11-26.39.1) should be included in the bill that stated: > *In performing its functions, [ASIS](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Secret_Intelligence_Service) must not engage in any conduct that would be contrary to Australia's obligations under the [Convention Against Torture](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_Against_Torture).* Attorney General [George Brandis](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/queensland/george_brandis) [said](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2014-11-26.26.1) that it was an unnecessary amendment. ### Background to the bill This [bill](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/s982) is the third that has been introduced since mid-2014. A number of incidents have happened before and during the course of the introduction of these bills. There was [one of the biggest counter-terrorism operations](http://www.abc.net.au/news/2014-09-18/authorities-thwart-beheading-plot-in-australias-biggest-raid/5754276) in Australian history. The Prime Minister [Tony Abbott](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/warringah/tony_abbott) also confirmed that Australia would be [sending the military to Iraq](http://www.abc.net.au/news/2014-10-15/special-forces-could-move-into-iraq-within-days-abbott/5815534) to fight the [Islamic State](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_State_of_Iraq_and_the_Levant) (IS) (also known as the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) or the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIL)). Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill (No. 1) 2014 - Third Reading - Pass the bill

speeches.speaker: Laurie Ferguson
speeches.brief: Reported that the committee considered 15 bills, found four compatible with human rights, deferred eight for further consideration and identified three requiring more information. Raised concerns that proposed disclosure of previous names on citizenship documents could threaten privacy, equality and safety, particularly for people fleeing violence or persecution.

speeches.speaker: Michael Keenan
speeches.brief: Introduced the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill (No. 1) 2014, which passed the Senate on 26 November, extends from four to eight hours the time the Australian Federal Police has to seek Attorney-General consent for an urgent interim control order, and said emergency ministerial authorisations for intelligence agencies would be strictly limited to 48 hours with no renewal.

speeches.speaker: Tony Pasin
speeches.brief: Supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill, argued that so-called lone wolf attacks are misleading since perpetrators often receive financial, logistical or planning support from others, and cited the recent attack on two police officers in Victoria and the attack on Canada's parliament as evidence of the evolving threat.

speeches.speaker: Tony Pasin
speeches.brief: Supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill (No. 1) 2014, explaining it allows agency heads to grant emergency authorisations for a maximum of 48 hours with the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security notified within three days, and extends control orders to those who enable or recruit for terrorism.

speeches.speaker: Ewen Jones
speeches.brief: Supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill, citing a UN Security Council resolution passed on 24 September 2014 requiring all 193 member states to prosecute foreign fighter recruitment, recounted his great-grandfather's 1902 experience of changing religion to get a public service job, and said 80 to 85 per cent of Australia's economy is services yet only 15 per cent of services are exported.

speeches.speaker: Scott Buchholz
speeches.brief: Supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill, citing ASIO data that 30 Australians trained with extremists in Afghanistan and Pakistan between 1990 and 2010, of whom 25 returned and eight were later convicted of terrorism offences, said up to 70 Australians are now fighting in Syria and Iraq with over 100 more supporting them, and explained the bill sets an eight-hour window for Attorney-General consent to urgent control orders.

speeches.speaker: Steve Irons
speeches.brief: Supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill, detailing the government's $630 million, four-year counter-terrorism package, 600 Australian Defence Force personnel and eight Super Hornets deployed in an advisory and strike role against Islamic State, and recalled the 18 September operation in Sydney and Brisbane that saw 15 people detained over an alleged public beheading plot.

speeches.speaker: Michael McCormack
speeches.brief: Supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill, describing an August visit to the Middle East with colleagues where Australian Defence Force head of operations Craig Orme stressed the importance of an ongoing regional presence, and criticised the member for Melbourne's opposition to the bill.

speeches.speaker: Philip Ruddock
speeches.brief: Supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill, noting the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security's 16 unanimous recommendations, quoted UK Home Secretary Theresa May's account of more than 500 British nationals travelling to Syria and Iraq and 40 terror plots foiled in the UK, and said around 70 young Australians are believed to have gone to the same conflict.

speeches.speaker: Karen McNamara
speeches.brief: Supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill, said more than a million Iraqis have been driven from their homes by Islamic State, recalled 88 Australians killed in the Bali bombings, and noted the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security tabled its advisory report on this bill on 20 November 2014.

speeches.speaker: Wyatt Roy
speeches.brief: Supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill, citing dozens of Australians fighting in Syria and Iraq and possibly more than 100 organisers and facilitators at home, and commended committee chair Dan Tehan for the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security's recommendations.

speeches.speaker: Jane Prentice
speeches.brief: Supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill, citing the Foreign Minister's advice that about 80 nations count foreign fighters among their citizens, said at least 70 Australians are on the ground with more than 100 suspected of funding or facilitating Daesh, and referenced the shock of seeing a 17-year-old Australian boy inciting terrorist ideologies.

speeches.speaker: Craig Kelly
speeches.brief: Supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill, said the government must find $13.5 billion a year just to pay interest on inherited Labor debt, recounted a 2009 plot to attack Holsworthy Army Barracks that was foiled after suspects were seen scouting Holsworthy railway station, and quoted sentencing judge Justice Betty King's rebuke of the plotters.

speeches.speaker: Rowan Ramsey
speeches.brief: Supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill, recalled that 202 people, including 88 Australians, died in the 2002 Bali bombing, noted Abdul Nacer Benbrika was jailed for 15 years in 2005 for plotting to bomb a football match with 11 others also convicted, and said an estimated 70 Australians are fighting in Syria and Iraq with more than 150 supporters at home.

speeches.speaker: Peter Hendy
speeches.brief: Supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill, citing an estimate of up to 170 Australians potentially fighting for Islamic State, a CIA assessment that IS fighter numbers in Iraq and Syria had risen to between 20,000 and 31,500, and a constituent's letter describing 30,000 to 40,000 Yazidi people stranded on Mount Sinjar without food or water.

speeches.speaker: Michael Sukkar
speeches.brief: Supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill, noting 149 members of the House backed it, credited committee chair Dan Tehan's Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security for balancing citizen protection with civil liberties, and argued the right to safety outweighs other considerations.

speeches.speaker: Eric Hutchinson
speeches.brief: Supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill, the third such bill since mid-2014, cited estimates of over 15,000 foreign nationals from countries including Australia fighting with Daesh in Iraq and Syria, and praised the Attorney-General's composed handling of a Q&A television appearance on the topic.

speeches.speaker: Lucy Wicks
speeches.brief: Began remarks supporting the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill by listing government achievements including a $12 billion infrastructure program featuring NorthConnex, and said the M1-M2 missing link would save 40,000 Central Coast commuters around 15 minutes each way while generating about 8,700 construction jobs.

speeches.speaker: Dennis Jensen
speeches.brief: Supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill, cited a Westpac survey finding 95 per cent of Western Australia's 209,000 firms are small businesses, credited a Greens amendment moved by Senator Penny Wright that reduced detention authorisation time from 12 to eight hours, and criticised Senator Leyonhjelm for opposing the bill.

speeches.speaker: Fiona Scott
speeches.brief: Supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill, cited United Nations Security Council resolution 2178 of 24 September calling on states to prevent foreign terrorist fighter travel, read out messages from Lindsay constituents supporting stronger security powers, and noted 13 of the committee's recommendations require only minor amendments to the bill.

speeches.speaker: Bert Van Manen
speeches.brief: Supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill, said the number of Australians fighting with or supporting terrorist groups grew from about 150 in June to 185 by the time of the bill, recalled the 18 September operation involving over 800 officers raiding 25 homes across Sydney and Brisbane including one in his own electorate of Forde, and referenced the fatal shooting of Canadian soldier Corporal Nathan Cirillo on 22 October.

speeches.speaker: Nola Marino
speeches.brief: Supported the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill (No. 1) 2014, describing measures to disrupt foreign fighters, expand control orders, assist military intelligence operations, provide emergency authorisations, retain metadata, and strengthen counter-radicalisation and financial controls.

speeches.speaker: Kelly O'Dwyer
speeches.brief: Supported the bill as part of a bipartisan response to Australians involved with terrorist groups overseas, highlighting expanded control orders, ASIS-ADF cooperation, emergency authorisations, and safeguards defining relevant classes of persons without reference to religion or ethnicity.

speeches.speaker: Dan Tehan
speeches.brief: Reported that the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security made 16 recommendations on the bill, including clearer control-order evidence, an eight-hour consent period, defined classes of Australian persons, and strengthened Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security oversight.
